job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Hana Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at 8:30 at the Northbank branch in Dunmore, where I'm a loan processing assistant. I check applications for missing documents, run the credit checks and prepare files for the loan officer, Mr. Adeyemi. Lunch is usually a sandwich with Bea from the cashiers' desk. I live in a rented flat with my cousin Ola, and we split the 900 rent. Evenings I do a bit of ironing, call my parents, who run a small shop two hours away, and try not to look at my loan balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about right, and good for me. At work I'd tell Mr. Adeyemi that the tool I use now and then to summarise documents saves me ten minutes a day, no more. With friends I'd say it's like every other technology, overpromised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my job is fairly safe but my money isn't. I'm on 23,800, my loan is about 40,000, and I've got barely three weeks of savings. If the bank closes the Dunmore branch, which they've been hinting at, I'd be moving anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, and use the time to move up from assistant to junior loan officer. I'd start the banking exam this winter, which costs 380, and I'd put 60 a month into savings. If the branch closed I'd ask for a transfer to the city. I'd also check how many suitable roles there are in the region, because I only know of two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady. It's the sort of future where my plan works if I do the work. I'm just aware the money margin is thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the branch might close. Has that been said officially?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not officially. Bea heard from someone at head office that some of the small branches are under review. It's a rumour, but rumours in banks tend to turn into emails. So I'd want to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first if the email came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr. Adeyemi straight away about a transfer and update my CV that night. Then I'd talk to Ola about whether we could stay in the flat or need to move. It's a small thing, but the flat is the one stable bit.

say: That's about right: the summary tool saves me ten **minutes** a day, no more.
think: My job is fairly safe but my money isn't: **40,000** of loan and about three weeks saved.
The branch may **close**, and then I'd have to move anyway.
do: Start the **banking exam** this winter, which costs 380.
Ask for a **transfer** to the city if the branch closes.
feel: Fairly **steady**; the plan works if I do the work, but the money margin is thin.
S0.quote: Rumours in banks tend to turn into emails.
fieldNote: Her fear is the **branch** closing, not AI, which fits a small-town bank job.
Planning is **concrete**: exam fee, monthly saving, transfer request.
Leans on **Ola** for housing, a quiet dependence.

steps.text: Start the banking exam this winter, which costs 380
Put 60 a month into a savings account
Ask Mr. Adeyemi for a transfer to a city branch if Dunmore closes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming and we should get ready, but not panic. At work I'd tell Mr. Adeyemi that our document checking is the kind of thing the card lists. I'd also tell friends to try the tools and see what's useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job changes the most. Checking documents and running credit checks is thinking work software already handles partly. The loan officers will still be needed, I think, because customers want a person to explain things. So the way up for me is to become that person, quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get good at the tools, properly, and be the one who teaches them to the team. I'd sign up for the banking exam and ask Mr. Adeyemi for a chance to handle small customer meetings. I'd keep my spending low and watch for jobs at the regional office. If the branch cut my hours, I'd ask Ola if we could rent out the sofa-bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense, mostly motivated. I like having a plan. What bothers me is the loan and how little room I've got for mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rent out the sofa-bed. How realistic is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's realistic, if awkward. It might bring in 150 a month from a student or someone on a short contract. Neither Ola nor I love the idea, but 150 a month is the difference between a savings pot and none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the branch would be hit hardest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bea and the other cashiers. Fewer people come in now, and if the bank leans on apps, they'll cut counter staff first. I'd want to help her think about moving into loans, but she's not keen on exams.

say: It's coming, so we should get **ready** but not panic.
I'd tell friends to **try** the tools and see what's useful.
think: My job changes the **most**, because document checking and credit checks are thinking work.
Customers still want a **person** to explain, so I need to become that person.
do: Get properly good at the **tools** and teach them to the team.
Sign up for the banking **exam** and ask Mr. Adeyemi for small customer meetings.
Rent out the **sofa-bed** if the branch cuts my hours.
feel: A bit **tense**, mostly motivated, with the loan leaving little room for mistakes.
S1.quote: 150 a month is the difference between a savings pot and none.
fieldNote: Sees the exit as becoming the **human** who explains loans.
Worries about **Bea**, the cashier, and wants to help but expects resistance.
Practical about **money**: sofa-bed rent, low spending.

steps.text: Learn the document tools properly and teach them to the Dunmore team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast for anyone to be ready, banks included. I'd say we need some rule on how quickly firms can swap people out. I'd say it carefully, because I don't want to be the one who made a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think most of my job goes in two years, and so does most of the loan officer's. A bank can run credit checks and file work with almost no staff. I'm 22 with 40,000 of debt, and I'd still owe it when my job's gone. I'd feel trapped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with money: cut spending to the bone, cancel the streaming and the gym, and ask the loan company about repayment relief. I'd keep working, learn whatever the bank offers and look for a job outside offices, like care or the public sector. I'd also ask my parents if I could help in their shop, though they can't pay me. I'd go home if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried sick, honestly. It's the type of worry that sits in your chest. I'd keep it from my parents until I knew more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really go back to your parents' shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it, but it'd be somewhere to live and eat while I worked out the next step. It's two hours away and they're not rich. I'd be a burden, and I'd feel I'd failed them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you try before that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few things: apply to the council, the health service admin, anywhere that hires people. I'd also ask Mr. Adeyemi if the bank has any plan for staff, like redeployment. If there's one, I'd want to be first in line.

say: Two years is too fast for anyone to be **ready**, banks included.
We need a rule on how quickly firms can **swap** people out.
think: Most of my job goes in two years, and so does most of the loan officer's work.
I'd still owe **40,000** when my job is gone, and I'd feel **trapped**.
do: Cut spending to the bone and ask the loan company about **relief**.
Look for jobs outside offices, like **care** or the public sector.
Ask Mr. Adeyemi about **redeployment** and go home to my parents' shop if I have to.
feel: **Worried sick**, in the chest, and I'd hide it from my parents until I knew more.
S2.quote: I'd hate it, but it'd be somewhere to live and eat while I worked out the next step.
fieldNote: Public **caution** hides private fear; she doesn't want to be seen making a fuss.
Going home would feel like **failing** her parents, a family-pride thread.
Looks for **public-sector** work and for redeployment first.

steps.text: Cancel streaming and the gym and cut spending to the bone
Ask the loan company for repayment relief
Apply to the council and health service admin jobs
Move back to my parents' flat above the shop if I lose my job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is some time, but not a lot. I'd say we should treat it as a deadline: banks to plan, governments to fund retraining. And I'd stay measured at work, not dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm anxious but have a chance. In five years I can maybe clear half my loan and be a loan officer on a better salary. If AGI really arrives in 2031 there'll be a squeeze, but I'd have savings and a little experience, which is better than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pass the banking exam in the first year and aim for a loan officer role by year two. I'd move the cheaper way: a flat share in the city or staying with Ola, whichever saves more. I'd overpay the loan by 100 a month. In year three I'd look sideways, maybe at financial advice or the public sector. I'd use AI at work more as it gets stronger, as long as it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Concerned, but with a bit of room. It feels like a clock that's ticking, not a bomb that's about to go off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave the bank before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw loan officers being cut in the region, or if the branch shut for good. I'd probably aim for a public body then, since they move slower and offer pensions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if you never got the loan officer job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd keep the processing role as long as possible and save more aggressively. I'd also ask myself whether it's time to try something quite different, like tax administration. I'd rather make a choice than have one made for me.

say: Five years is some time but not a lot, so treat it as a **deadline**.
I'd stay **measured** at work, not dramatic.
think: I'm anxious but have a **chance**: half the loan cleared and a better salary by then.
There will be a **squeeze** in 2031, but savings and experience would help.
do: Pass the **banking exam** in year one and aim for loan officer by year two.
Overpay the loan by **100 a month**.
In year three look at **financial advice** or the public sector.
feel: Concerned but with room: a **clock** ticking, not a bomb about to go off.
S3.quote: I'd rather make a choice than have one made for me.
fieldNote: Wants to **choose** rather than be chosen for, a steady stance.
Names the **public sector** as a slower, safer move.
Plans are **sequenced** by year, practical and evidence-led.

steps.text: Pass the banking exam in the first year
Aim for a junior loan officer role by year two
Overpay the student loan by 100 a month
Use proven AI tools at work as they improve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means we can do this properly: training, rules and a fair share of the gains. I'd say let's not waste it arguing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fairly okay. By 32 I could be a senior loan officer or in advice, with the loan paid and a deposit saved. The worry would be that things move faster than the card says, and I'd have less warning than I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the banking exam and the loan officer role over the first three years. I'd pay off the loan by about 28, then save for a deposit. Around year five I'd consider moving to a regulator or a consumer body, which are more stable. I'd also try new AI tools as they become standard, but not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A small voice says not to trust it completely, but it's a good feeling to have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the small voice say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That forecasts are guesses. If it came faster, I'd be in the same boat as the two-year world. So I'd keep a savings cushion, just in case, and keep my CV updated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change when you think about starting a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. With ten years I'd think about kids by 30, once the loan's done. In the two-year world I'd put it off indefinitely. Having time lets me plan a normal life.

think: By 32 I could be a senior loan officer with the loan paid and a **deposit** saved.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years isn't enough to get a better job and shrink the loan, and the bank might not wait. What would help is a clear warning from employers and a retraining offer that doesn't make me take on more debt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say people assume graduates are fine because we have degrees. A degree is just a debt with a certificate on it, until the job is there.

headlineQuote: A degree is just a debt with a certificate on it, until the job is there.
portrait: **Hana** is 22, a finance graduate working as a loan processing assistant at a small bank branch in Dunmore.
She owes about **40,000**, has three weeks of savings and shares a rented flat with her cousin.
She is a centrist and uses AI now and then, adopting it once it's **proven**.
She plans in steps: banking exam, loan officer role, then the **public sector** if the bank wobbles.
Her family can't help, so more time is what makes her feel **safe**.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because two years isn't enough to move up and shrink the loan.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **warning** from employers and retraining that doesn't add more debt.
